Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.37 6 The Three Isomorphism Theorems If G and H are groups and ϕ ∶ G → H is a homomorphism with kernel K, we know from Proposition 5.2.4 that K ⊴ G; therefore G/K is a group by Definition 5.1.1. Recall that, G/K = {gK ∶ g ∈ G}. Theorem 6.0.1. (The First Isomorphism Theorem) Let G and H be groups and let ϕ ∶ G → H be a homomorphism with kernel K and image I. Then, G / K ≅ I. The isomorphism is the map θ ∶ G/K → I given by θ(gK) = ϕ(g). Proof. We must first check that: (i) θ is a function (i.e. if g1K = g2K, then we must show that θ(g1K) = θ(g2K) because a function can’t map the same thing to two different things. (This is called being well-defined). Proof: if g1K = g2K, then g−1 1 g2 ∈ K by Theorem 4.1.3, and so ϕ(g−1 1 g2) = eH . Since ϕ is a homomor- phism, this implies that ϕ(g1) = ϕ(g2). Hence θ(g1K) = θ(g2K), so θ is well-defined. (ii) θ is a homomorphism. Proof: This is easy. Indeed, θ((g1K)(g2K)) = θ((g1g2)K) = ϕ(g1g2) = ϕ(g1)ϕ(g2) = θ((g1K)θ((g2K). (iii) θ is onto. Proof: This is easy. Indeed, any element in I is of the form ϕ(g) for some g ∈ G, and is therefore equal to θ(gK). (iv) θ is one-to-one. Proof: θ(g1K) = θ(g2K) ⟹ ϕ(g1) = ϕ(g2) ⟹ ϕ(g−1 1 g2) = eH ⟹ g−1 1 g2 ∈ K. But g−1 1 g2 ∈ K implies (by Theorem 4.1.3) that g1K = g2K. Definition 6.0.2. Let G be a group with N ⊴ G. The map π ∶ G → G/N given by π(g) = gN is a homomorphism (exercise - check this) and obviously has kernel N and image G/N . It is often called the canonical homomorphism. Example 6.0.3. Fix n ∈ N. Recall Example 5.2.2, where we proved the map φ ∶ Z → Zn given by φ(m) = [m]n is a homomorphism. We also proved: • Ker(φ) = nZ = the set of multiples of n • Im(φ) = Zn. Using the First Isomorphism Theorem we can deduce that Z/nZ ≅ Zn. We already proved this directly in Example 5.1.2 for n = 3. Now we see this phenomena is true for all n ∈ N. Theorem 6.0.4. (The Second Isomorphism Theorem) Let G be a group with H ≤ G and N ⊴ G. Then the following quotient groups are isomorphic: H/(H ∩ N ) ≅ (HN )/N. The next theorem is sometimes called “The Fool’s Cancellation Theorem” because it looks like the groups can be “cancelled” like integers. Theorem 6.0.5. (The Third Isomorphism Theorem) Let G be a group with N ⊴ G. If M ⊴ G and N ≤ M ≤ G, then M /N ⊴ G/N and the following quotient groups are isomorphic: (G/N )/(M /N ) ≅ G/M.

# Page 2^page=2
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.38 6.0.1 Handout for Section 6 Proof of The Second Isomorphism Theorem. Let ϕ ∶ H → (HN )/N be the map given by ϕ(h) = hN . (i) It is easy to prove that this is a homomorphism. (ii) The kernel is K = {h ∈ H ∶ hN = eHN /N } = {h ∈ H ∶ hN = N } = {h ∈ H ∶ h ∈ N } = H ∩ N . (iii) The image is I = {hN ∈ (HN )/N ∶ h ∈ H} = {hkN ∈ (HN )/N ∶ h ∈ H, k ∈ N } = (HN )/N . (iv) Result follows immediately from the First Isomorphism Theorem. Proof of the Third Isomorphism Theorem. Let ϕ ∶ G/N → G/M be the map given by ϕ(gN ) = gM . (i) It is easy to prove this is a homomorphism. (ii) The kernel is K = {hN ∶ hM = M } = {hN ∶ h ∈ M } = M /N . (iii) The image is I = {gM ∶ gN ∈ G/N } = {gM ∶ g ∈ G} = G/M . (iv) Result follows immediately from the First Isomorphism Theorem.

Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.41 7 A new permutation group: the alternating group 7.1 Cycle shape In this section we will define an important homomorphism (called the signature function) on Sn. The kernel of this function is called the alternating group and is one of the most important groups in the course—we will explore this group in the next section. Before defining the signature function, we first introduce cycle shape. In the next section we will see how to use the cycle shapes to quickly calculate the signature function. Definition 7.1.1. The cycle shape of a permutation just tells you how long its cycles are when written as a product of disjoint cycles. Formally, let g ∈ Sn be a permutation that is not the identity. We can write g as a product of disjoint cycles, g = c1c2⋯cm, where each cycle ci has length ri and r1 ≥ r2 ≥ ⋯ ≥ rm. The cycle shape of g is then (r1, r2, . . . , rm). The cycle shape of the identity is usually taken to be ∅. Example 7.1.2. Here are some examples of cycle shape. 1. The cycle shape of g = (1 3 5 7 2 9)(4 8)(10 6 12 11) ∈ S12 is (6, 4, 2) because g is comprised of a cycle of length 6, another of length 4 and one of length 2. (Notice that we reordered the cycles before describing the shape.) 2. The cycle shape of h = (1 2)(3 4)(7 8)(9 10) ∈ S10 is (2, 2, 2, 2) Question 7.1.3. What are all the cycle shapes that occur in S4? For any permutation in S4 (written as a product of disjoint cycles) we have that each number in {1, 2, 3, 4} lies in precisely one cycle (possible a cycle of length one). Cycle shape List of elements in S4 with this cycle shape No. elements ∅ e 1 (2) (1 2), (1 3), (1 4), (2 3), (2 4), (3 4) 6 (2, 2) (1 2)(3 4), (1 3)(2 4), (1 4)(2 3) 3 (3) (1 2 3), (1 3 2), (1 2 4), (1 4 2), (1 3 4), (1 4 3), 8 (2 3 4), (2 4 3) (4) (1 2 3 4), (1 2 4 3), (1 3 2 4), (1 3 4 2), 6 (1 4 2 3), (1 4 3 2) We have definitely found everything because ∣S4∣ = 4! = 24.
